title: Microplastics field project
context: You will hear three geography students, Lena, Callum and Josh, planning a group project on microplastics in a local river.

lines.t: OK, so we need to finalise the sampling procedure today, otherwise we'll never get started. We agreed on four sites along the river, right?
Yes, but I've been looking at the map again, and the one upstream of the town is a problem. There's no proper way down to the water, just a steep bank.
I'd suggest choosing sites near the bridges, because they're easy to find.

Easy to find, maybe, but you can't stand on a bridge and collect a sample properly. I think the rule should be that every site has to be close to a footpath. That way we can get there safely, even in bad weather.
That's sensible. I'll pick four that fit.
Then there's the collection itself. I still think the simplest thing is to fill some glass jars directly from the river.
The trouble is, a jar only holds about a litre, and microplastics are spread pretty thinly. We'd hardly find anything. We need to filter a much larger volume of water.
So we use the fine mesh net from the department. You hold it in the current for ten minutes and it catches everything bigger than a third of a millimetre.
Fair enough, the net it is. Then we rinse what's in the net into a container.
And it has to be a glass container, not a plastic one. Otherwise we'd risk contamination, and the whole thing would be pointless.
Good point. Back in the lab we pass the sample through filter paper. Then the paper needs to dry. I thought we could just leave it on a windowsill overnight.
Dust would get onto it though, and some of that dust could be synthetic fibres from clothing. I'd rather put it in the oven in lab three. It's only forty degrees, so it won't damage anything.
Agreed. And the last step is counting the particles under the microscope and noting the colour and shape of each one.
Great. You know, people keep asking why we chose this topic. Everyone assumes it's because of that article in the local paper last month.
Which was a nice coincidence. But honestly, the main reason was that the department already had all the equipment we needed, so we didn't have to spend anything.
True. And Dr Moss had suggested a soil project, remember, which we weren't keen on. Now, timing. When do we actually go out?
I'd like to sample straight after heavy rain, because that's when rubbish gets washed off the roads into the river.
But we can't plan our lives around the forecast. It's been wrong all week. I'd rather go on the same day every week for four weeks. If one of those happens to follow rain, we just make a note of it.
I suppose that's more systematic. OK, once a week for a month.
Then who does what? I don't mind doing the data analysis.
Actually, Callum, you're the best writer of the three of us. Josh did the advanced statistics module, so wouldn't it make more sense if he did the analysis and you wrote it up?
I'm happy with that. I'll take the analysis.
Fine, I'll write the report, then. Should we end it with some recommendations for the council?

From four weeks of data? I think that's a bit ambitious. What would be useful is to compare our results with a published study on a similar river. There's one from Scotland that used the same mesh size.
Yes, that would give our numbers some context. Let's do that. I'd love to include photos of the particles as well, but the camera on the microscope is broken.
Oh well. Is there anything I need to do before Monday? Do we need to book the lab?

I booked it yesterday. And the department lends out waterproof boots, so we don't need to buy those. But someone has to get the risk assessment signed by the technician before we're allowed near the water.
I'll do that tomorrow morning, then.

items.evidence: Fair enough, the net it is.

items.explanation: A plastic container would risk contamination.

items.evidence: counting the particles under the microscope

The necessary equipment was already available.
optionNotes: The article was 'a nice coincidence', not the reason.
Dr Moss suggested a soil project instead.

once a week for four weeks
on a single day at all four sites
optionNotes: Josh's idea, rejected because the forecast is unreliable.

items.evidence: OK, once a week for a month.
